title: Pulmonary Pathogens
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the bacteria, viruses, and fungi that infect the lungs, with the structural features, laboratory traits, and virulence factors that identify each and explain the disease it causes. Board questions usually give a host or exposure clue (asplenia, alcohol use, cystic fibrosis, a cooling tower, a cave, a CD4 count) and ask for the organism, its toxin, its culture requirement, or how it escapes immunity. If you can connect each organism's biology to the defense it defeats, you can reason through these questions instead of memorizing lists, and you will recognize why particular patients get particular infections.
prerequisites: Gram-positive and gram-negative cell wall structure and the Gram stain
Complement, opsonization, and splenic clearance of bacteria (IM-7, IM-8)
Th1 cell-mediated immunity, macrophage activation, and granuloma formation (IM-5, IM-13)
G protein signaling: Gs, Gi, adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP
Respiratory tract defenses: mucociliary clearance and alveolar macrophages (PU-2, PU-12)

connections.to: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system (PU-14-H)
connections.how: The pneumonias, tuberculosis, and fungal diseases taught there are the clinical expression of the organisms described here.
Falling CD4 counts in HIV infection predict which lung pathogens appear, with Pneumocystis below 200 cells/mm3.

connections.to: Complement and lymphatic organ function (IM-7, IM-8)
connections.how: Encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae are cleared by opsonization and the spleen, so asplenia and complement defects raise risk.
CFTR mutations thicken airway mucus, which explains chronic Pseudomonas colonization in cystic fibrosis.
Pertussis and cholera toxins both raise cAMP but act on opposite G proteins, a common comparison on board questions.

terms.def: Coating of a microbe with antibody or complement C3b so phagocytes can bind and ingest it.
A loose carbohydrate layer outside the cell wall that hides the bacterium from complement and phagocytes.
Acquisition of a new trait, such as a toxin gene, from a bacteriophage integrated into the bacterial chromosome.
Enzymatic transfer of ADP-ribose from NAD+ onto a host protein, which changes or abolishes that protein's function.
Retaining carbolfuchsin stain after decolorizing with acid alcohol, a property of bacteria with mycolic acid-rich walls.
Dried respiratory particles about 1 to 5 um across that stay airborne and reach the alveoli when inhaled.
A compact collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), giant cells, and lymphocytes that walls off a persistent antigen.
Gradual change in viral surface antigens from point mutations, producing seasonal epidemics.
Abrupt replacement of an influenza A surface antigen by reassortment of genome segments, which can produce a pandemic.
A multinucleated cell formed when a viral fusion protein on an infected cell fuses it with neighboring cells.
A fungus that grows as a mold in the environment and converts to a yeast or spherule at body temperature.
Growth of fungal hyphae into blood vessel walls, causing thrombosis and hemorrhagic infarction of tissue.

blocks.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is a gram-positive coccus that grows in pairs of lancet-shaped cells, called diplococci. It colonizes the nasopharynx of many healthy people, and disease follows when it reaches a site where it is not promptly cleared: the alveoli after aspiration of nasopharyngeal secretions, or the middle ear, sinuses, blood, or meninges. It is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia and the classic cause of lobar pneumonia, in which consolidation fills an entire lobe.
Laboratory identification

Like all streptococci it is catalase negative. On blood agar it is alpha-hemolytic: hydrogen peroxide made by the organism oxidizes hemoglobin to a green product, leaving a zone of partial hemolysis. Viridans streptococci look the same, so two tests separate them. Optochin inhibits pneumococcal growth around a disk, while viridans streptococci are resistant. In the bile solubility test, bile salts activate the pneumococcal autolysin (LytA), which digests the cell wall and lyses the colony; viridans streptococci do not lyse. The capsule also swells visibly when mixed with type-specific antiserum (the quellung reaction).

blocks.title: Virulence factors of S. pneumoniae
rows: Polysaccharide capsule (about 100 serotypes)
Hydrophilic coat limits C3b deposition and hides deposited C3b and antibody from phagocyte receptors
Resists phagocytosis; clearance needs type-specific antibody and the spleen
IgA protease
Cleaves secretory IgA1 at its hinge region
Allows colonization of the nasopharyngeal mucosa
Pneumolysin
Cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin; also activates complement
Damages alveolar epithelium and endothelium, slows cilia, intensifies inflammation
Autolysin (LytA)
Lyses the bacterium, releasing pneumolysin and cell wall fragments
Cell wall teichoic acid and peptidoglycan trigger strong innate inflammation
blocks.caption: The capsule is the essential virulence factor; unencapsulated strains are rarely invasive.

blocks.text: Because the capsule blocks complement-mediated uptake, defense depends on anticapsular IgG that opsonizes the organism and on splenic macrophages that remove poorly opsonized bacteria from the blood. Capsular polysaccharide is a T cell-independent antigen, so children under about 2 years respond poorly to it. People with asplenia, whether surgical or functional as in sickle cell disease, and people with antibody or C3 deficiency are at risk for rapid, overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis.
Lobar pneumonia

Bacteria multiply in the alveoli and the protein-rich edema fluid they provoke carries them through the pores of Kohn to neighboring alveoli, so infection spreads through a lobe until stopped by the pleura of the fissures. The pathologic stages follow the inflammatory response.

blocks.title: Stages of lobar pneumonia
steps: Congestion: vascular engorgement, edema fluid, many bacteria (about days 1 to 2)
Red hepatization: neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin fill alveoli
Gray hepatization: red cells lyse; fibrinosuppurative exudate remains
Resolution: enzymes digest exudate, macrophages clear debris
blocks.caption: Approximate timing follows Robbins; with resolution the alveolar architecture is usually restored.

blocks.text: The manifestations follow from these stages. Abrupt fever and rigors reflect cytokine release, and rust-colored sputum reflects red cells and degraded hemoglobin in the exudate. Consolidated lung is airless, so it is dull to percussion, and it transmits sound well, producing bronchial breath sounds and increased tactile fremitus. Alveoli that are perfused but filled with exudate act as a shunt, causing hypoxemia, and extension to the pleura causes pleuritic pain. Bacteremia can seed the meninges or joints.

blocks.predict: A 19-year-old with sickle cell disease develops fever and becomes hypotensive within hours. Which organism should you think of first, and why is she vulnerable?
blocks.explain: Repeated splenic infarction leaves her functionally asplenic, so poorly opsonized encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae are not removed from the blood.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on capsule and host defense.

blocks.text: Four gram-negative organisms account for most board questions on gram-negative pneumonia. Each has a growth requirement or structural trait that identifies it in the laboratory and a host or exposure setting that explains who gets it.

blocks.title: Gram-negative lung pathogens compared
rows: Haemophilus influenzae
Small pleomorphic coccobacillus
Needs factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD+); grows on chocolate agar; satellite growth around S. aureus
Type b capsule (polyribosylribitol phosphate); IgA protease
Type b: invasive disease in unvaccinated young children; nontypeable: otitis, sinusitis, COPD exacerbations
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Nonmotile rod; lactose fermenter (mucoid pink colonies on MacConkey agar)
Very mucoid colonies; urease positive
Large polysaccharide capsule
Aspiration in alcohol use disorder and diabetes; hospital-acquired infection
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Aerobic rod; non-lactose fermenter
Oxidase positive; blue-green pigment (pyocyanin); grape-like odor
Exotoxin A (ADP-ribosylates EF-2); alginate biofilm; type III secretion
Cystic fibrosis, mechanical ventilation, neutropenia, burns
Legionella pneumophila
Rod that stains poorly with Gram stain; facultative intracellular
Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with iron and cysteine; urine antigen (serogroup 1)
Multiplies inside macrophages in a vacuole that avoids lysosomes
Aerosols from contaminated warm water; older smokers, chronic lung disease, immunosuppression
blocks.caption: Each organism favors a setting in which a specific host defense is weakened or bypassed.

blocks.text: H. influenzae cannot synthesize heme (factor X), which it needs for its cytochromes, or NAD+ (factor V). Chocolate agar supplies both because heating lyses the red cells to release them and inactivates enzymes in blood that degrade NAD+. On ordinary blood agar it grows only beside a hemolytic S. aureus streak, which supplies NAD+ and releases heme (satellite growth). The type b capsule, like the pneumococcal capsule, resists complement and allows bloodstream invasion, causing meningitis, epiglottitis, and bacteremia in young children who lack anticapsular antibody. Nontypeable strains lack a capsule, stay on mucosal surfaces, and exploit damaged mucociliary clearance in COPD.

Klebsiella pneumonia usually follows aspiration of oral secretions colonized by gram-negative rods in people whose cough and gag reflexes are blunted by alcohol. Its thick capsule resists phagocytosis, and the infection is destructive, producing necrosis, abscesses, and thick, bloody, mucoid sputum described as currant jelly.

Pseudomonas thrives in moist environments, including respiratory equipment. An endotracheal tube bypasses upper airway defenses and carries a biofilm, which explains ventilator-associated pneumonia. In cystic fibrosis, dehydrated mucus from defective CFTR is poorly cleared; Pseudomonas colonizes it, switches to a mucoid alginate-producing form, and grows in biofilms that resist antibodies and neutrophils. The persistent neutrophil response damages bronchial walls and causes bronchiectasis. Exotoxin A kills cells by the same reaction as diphtheria toxin (C03).

Legionella lives inside free-living amoebae in warm water systems such as cooling towers, hot water plumbing, and whirlpools, and infects people who inhale aerosols; it is not spread person to person. In alveolar macrophages it uses a secretion system to build a vacuole that escapes lysosomal fusion, so control requires cell-mediated immunity. Legionnaires disease is a severe pneumonia with high fever and frequent diarrhea, confusion, and hyponatremia; Pontiac fever is a self-limited influenza-like illness without pneumonia. Because it stains poorly, a gram stain of sputum shows neutrophils but few organisms.

Diphtheria toxin and pertussis toxin are both AB toxins: a binding (B) portion attaches to host cells and delivers an active (A) portion that is an ADP-ribosyltransferase. The A portion transfers ADP-ribose from NAD+ onto a specific host protein. The disease each causes follows from which protein is modified.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae

C. diphtheriae is a gram-positive, club-shaped, pleomorphic rod that often lies in V and L shapes and contains metachromatic (polyphosphate) granules. It forms black colonies on tellurite-containing agar. Only strains lysogenized by a bacteriophage (corynephage beta) carrying the tox gene make toxin, an example of lysogenic conversion. A bacterial repressor (DtxR) blocks tox transcription when iron is plentiful, so toxin is made when iron is scarce. Toxin production by an isolate is confirmed with the Elek immunodiffusion test.

blocks.title: Diphtheria toxin from phage to tissue damage
steps: Phage carrying tox gene lysogenizes C. diphtheriae
Bacteria colonize pharynx and secrete toxin; they stay local
B fragment binds the HB-EGF precursor receptor; toxin is endocytosed
Endosomal acid moves the A fragment into the cytosol
A fragment ADP-ribosylates EF-2; protein synthesis stops; cells die
Absorbed toxin reaches the myocardium and peripheral nerves
blocks.caption: Elongation factor 2 (EF-2) moves the ribosome along mRNA; a single A fragment can halt translation in a cell.

blocks.text: Local cell death produces a pseudomembrane of necrotic epithelium, fibrin, neutrophils, and bacteria on the tonsils, pharynx, or larynx. It is gray, adherent, and bleeds when scraped, and it can obstruct the airway. Edema and cervical lymphadenopathy give the bull neck. Circulating toxin causes myocarditis with conduction block, typically in the first or second week, and a demyelinating neuropathy that often begins with palatal paralysis and cranial nerve palsies.
Bordetella pertussis

B. pertussis is a small, strictly aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus grown on Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe agar. It attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium with filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin but does not invade. Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates the alpha subunit of Gi. The modified Gi can no longer be activated by its receptors, so it cannot inhibit adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP rises. Because chemokine receptors signal through Gi, lymphocytes fail to leave the blood, producing marked lymphocytosis; phagocyte recruitment and killing are impaired, and in infants increased insulin release can cause hypoglycemia. A second toxin, adenylate cyclase toxin, enters phagocytes and makes cAMP itself, while tracheal cytotoxin, a peptidoglycan fragment, kills ciliated cells and cripples mucociliary clearance.

blocks.title: Clinical stages of pertussis
rows: Catarrhal
1 to 2 weeks
Rhinorrhea, mild cough, low fever; highest bacterial load, most contagious
Paroxysmal
2 to 6 weeks
Bursts of cough, then an inspiratory whoop through a narrowed glottis; post-tussive vomiting; infants may have apnea instead
Convalescent
Weeks to months
Cough fades slowly as ciliated epithelium regenerates
blocks.caption: The cough outlasts the bacteria because toxin-damaged epithelium takes weeks to recover.

blocks.title: Worked example: four toxins, two targets
blocks.text: Pertussis toxin and cholera toxin both raise cAMP, so why do they differ? Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha and blocks its GTPase, so Gs stays bound to GTP and keeps stimulating adenylyl cyclase: the accelerator is stuck down. Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi alpha so receptors cannot activate it, and the inhibitory signal is lost: the brake is cut. Both end with high cAMP, but in different cells with different results (intestinal chloride secretion versus lymphocytosis and phagocyte dysfunction). Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A use the same ADP-ribosylation reaction on a different target, EF-2, so their result is not altered signaling but halted protein synthesis and cell death.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slender, nonmotile, obligately aerobic rod that divides only about once every 15 to 20 hours, so culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium takes several weeks. Its defining feature is a thick, waxy cell wall in which long-chain mycolic acids are linked to arabinogalactan and peptidoglycan. This lipid-rich wall stains poorly with the Gram stain, resists drying and detergents, and slows the entry of nutrients and many antibiotics.

In the Ziehl-Neelsen stain, heated carbolfuchsin penetrates the waxy wall, and acid alcohol then fails to remove it, so the bacilli stay red against a blue counterstain: they are acid-fast. Fluorescent auramine-rhodamine staining relies on the same wall lipids.

blocks.title: Cell wall components and what they do
rows: Mycolic acids
Form a waxy, hydrophobic outer layer
Acid-fast staining; resistance to drying, disinfectants, and many drugs
Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate)
Activates macrophages to release TNF-alpha; toxic to host cell mitochondria; inhibits neutrophil migration
Granuloma formation; virulent strains grow in serpentine cords in culture
Sulfatides
Sulfated glycolipids that inhibit phagosome and lysosome fusion
Bacilli survive inside macrophages
Lipoarabinomannan
Arrests phagosome maturation and dampens macrophage activation
Adds to intracellular survival
blocks.caption: The wall lipids explain the staining, the intracellular survival, and much of the inflammation.

blocks.text: Transmission and intracellular survival

A person with active pulmonary disease, especially with cavities, expels respiratory droplets when coughing or talking. As they dry they become droplet nuclei about 1 to 5 um across, which stay suspended in room air for hours and are small enough to pass the mucociliary escalator and reach the alveoli. A few bacilli are enough to start infection. Larger droplets are trapped in the upper airway and cleared, which is why crowded, poorly ventilated spaces matter more than brief contact.

Alveolar macrophages ingest the bacilli, but the organism arrests phagosome maturation: the phagosome excludes the proton pump, stays near neutral pH, and does not fuse with lysosomes. The bacilli multiply inside the macrophage and spread through lymphatics and blood before adaptive immunity develops. After about 3 weeks, Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to complete phagolysosome fusion, produce nitric oxide, and kill the bacilli. TNF-alpha recruits cells and holds the granuloma together.

blocks.title: Primary tuberculosis infection
steps: Droplet nuclei carry bacilli to alveoli
Macrophages ingest bacilli; phagolysosome fusion is blocked
Bacilli multiply and spread to hilar nodes
Dendritic cells and macrophages release IL-12; Th1 cells develop
IFN-gamma activates macrophages to kill bacilli
Caseating granulomas form: Ghon focus plus hilar nodes (Ghon complex)
Most lesions heal, fibrose, and calcify, leaving latent infection
blocks.caption: The same Th1 response makes the tuberculin skin test positive, a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

blocks.text: The primary (Ghon) focus is a small subpleural lesion in the lower part of an upper lobe or the upper part of a lower lobe, the well-ventilated zones where inhaled particles land. Reactivation occurs when cell-mediated immunity weakens, as in HIV infection, malnutrition, older age, or glucocorticoid use, and it favors the apical posterior segments of the upper lobes. Their high ventilation-perfusion ratio gives the highest alveolar PO2, which suits an obligate aerobe. Caseous necrosis liquefies, drains into a bronchus, and leaves a cavity rich in bacilli; erosion of vessels causes hemoptysis. Fever, night sweats, and weight loss reflect TNF-alpha and IL-1.

blocks.predict: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis and a positive tuberculin test years ago starts a drug that neutralizes TNF-alpha. What might happen in the lungs, and why?
blocks.explain: TNF-alpha maintains the granulomas that contain latent bacilli; without it they break down and latent infection reactivates, often as disseminated disease.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraphs on intracellular survival and the primary infection flow.

sections.title: Influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and coronaviruses

blocks.caption: All three are enveloped. Negative-sense viruses must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; a positive-sense genome is translated directly.

blocks.text: Influenza

Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium; after endocytosis, endosomal acid changes its shape so it fuses the envelope with the endosome membrane. Hemagglutinin must first be cleaved by host proteases, which helps restrict infection to the respiratory tract. Unusually for an RNA virus, influenza replicates in the nucleus, where its polymerase takes 5' caps from host pre-mRNA to prime viral mRNA. Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release new virions. Antibody to hemagglutinin neutralizes infection.

The viral polymerase has no proofreading, so point mutations accumulate in the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes. This antigenic drift allows partial escape from existing antibody and causes yearly epidemics of influenza A and B. Influenza A also infects birds and pigs, and when two strains infect one cell their segments can reassort. Antigenic shift introduces a hemagglutinin (or neuraminidase) subtype against which the population has little immunity, and pandemics follow.

blocks.title: Antigenic shift in influenza A
steps: Human and animal influenza A strains circulate separately
Both strains infect one host cell, often in a pig
Segments are packaged in new combinations (reassortment)
A virion carries a novel hemagglutinin subtype and human-adapted genes
Little population immunity: rapid worldwide spread (pandemic)
blocks.caption: Shift requires a segmented genome and animal reservoirs.

blocks.text: Influenza kills ciliated tracheobronchial epithelium and strips away mucociliary clearance, so upper airway bacteria (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) can cause secondary pneumonia, often after initial improvement.
RSV

RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia in infants. Its F protein, displayed on infected cells, fuses them with their neighbors to form syncytia. Necrotic epithelium, mucus, and edema plug the bronchioles. Because resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius, slight narrowing of an infant's small bronchioles sharply raises resistance, causing wheezing, air trapping, and hypoxemia.
Coronaviruses

Coronaviruses have among the largest RNA virus genomes and, unlike most RNA viruses, a proofreading exonuclease. The genome is translated directly into polyproteins that viral proteases cleave into the replication complex. Seasonal coronaviruses cause common colds. SARS-CoV-2 spike binds ACE2, and host proteases (furin and TMPRSS2) cleave spike to allow fusion; MERS coronavirus instead uses DPP4. ACE2 is present on nasal epithelium, type II pneumocytes, endothelium, and enterocytes. Severe COVID-19 causes diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes, endothelial injury, and microvascular thrombosis. Loss of smell reflects infection of supporting cells of the olfactory epithelium.

blocks.title: Worked example: drift or shift?
blocks.text: Outbreak 1: a winter influenza A epidemic in which most adults have some antibody, but this year's hemagglutinin differs from last year's by a few amino acids. Outbreak 2: a new hemagglutinin subtype appears in humans after a pig strain exchanges segments with a human strain, and illness spreads worldwide in all ages. Outbreak 1 is drift: point mutations from an error-prone polymerase allow partial escape, so prior immunity still blunts severity. Outbreak 2 is shift: reassortment brings in an antigen no one has met. Ask whether the change is gradual or abrupt and whether it needs exchanged segments. Only influenza A, with animal reservoirs, shifts; influenza B only drifts.

The endemic dimorphic fungi grow in soil as molds at environmental temperatures and convert to a tissue form at body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F). People inhale conidia from disturbed soil, so geography and exposure history are the main clues. The tissue form is how the pathologist identifies each fungus.

blocks.title: Endemic dimorphic fungi
rows: Histoplasma capsulatum
Ohio and Mississippi River valleys; soil enriched by bird and bat droppings (caves, chicken coops, old buildings)
Small oval yeasts, about 2 to 4 um, inside macrophages
Calcified granulomas that mimic tuberculosis; dissemination with hepatosplenomegaly, oral ulcers, pancytopenia in AIDS
Blastomyces dermatitidis
Great Lakes and Ohio and Mississippi River basins; moist soil and decaying wood near waterways
Large yeasts, about 8 to 15 um, with a thick refractile wall and a single broad-based bud
Pneumonia; spread to skin (verrucous lesions), bone, and prostate; mixed suppurative and granulomatous inflammation
Coccidioides immitis and posadasii
Southwestern United States (Arizona, California's San Joaquin Valley) and northern Mexico; desert soil dust
Spherules, about 20 to 60 um or larger, filled with endospores (not a yeast)
Erythema nodosum and arthralgias; spread to skin, bone, and meninges
blocks.caption: All three are acquired by inhalation and are not spread person to person; most infections are mild or silent.

blocks.text: Defense against all three is cell-mediated. Alveolar macrophages ingest the inhaled conidia or yeasts, and Th1 cells release IFN-gamma that activates macrophages and organizes granulomas, much as in tuberculosis. The usual result is a self-limited pneumonia or silent infection that heals with calcified granulomas. Disseminated disease occurs mainly when T cell immunity is impaired, as in advanced HIV infection, transplantation, or glucocorticoid use.

Each fungus has a feature that shapes its disease. Histoplasma yeasts survive and multiply within macrophage phagosomes, so they travel with macrophages through the reticuloendothelial system to the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow. Blastomyces spreads mainly through the blood, most often to skin and bone. Coccidioides spherules are too large for macrophages to ingest; when a spherule ruptures it releases many endospores, each of which can form a new spherule and attracts neutrophils.

blocks.title: Coccidioides in soil and tissue
steps: Mold in desert soil produces barrel-shaped arthroconidia
Wind and dust carry arthroconidia into the lungs
Each arthroconidium enlarges into a spherule at body temperature
Endospores develop inside the spherule
Spherule ruptures; each endospore forms a new spherule
blocks.caption: Endospores amplify infection within tissue; arthroconidia form only in the environmental mold phase.

blocks.text: Erythema nodosum in coccidioidomycosis, and in some cases of histoplasmosis, is an immune reaction to fungal antigen rather than skin infection, and it marks a vigorous cell-mediated response. Coccidioides disseminates more often in pregnancy (especially the third trimester), in immunosuppression, and in people of Filipino or African ancestry.

Aspergillus and Pneumocystis are opportunists: healthy people inhale them often without disease, and serious infection appears when a specific defense is missing. Knowing which defense controls each organism predicts which patient will be infected.

blocks.caption: The host defect predicts the organism: a missing neutrophil suggests Aspergillus, a missing CD4 T cell suggests Pneumocystis.

blocks.text: Aspergillus

Aspergillus conidia are about 2 to 3 um across and reach the alveoli. Alveolar macrophages normally kill them, and any conidia that germinate are killed as hyphae by neutrophils, which use NADPH oxidase products and granule contents. When neutrophils are absent or dysfunctional, as in prolonged neutropenia, chronic granulomatous disease (phagocytes lacking NADPH oxidase), or high-dose glucocorticoid use, hyphae grow freely and invade blood vessels. The resulting thrombosis and infarction cause nodules surrounded by hemorrhage, hemoptysis, and pleuritic pain, and the fungus can spread to the brain.

In tissue, Aspergillus hyphae are narrow, regularly septate, and branch at acute angles. Mucorales (such as Rhizopus and Mucor), which also invade vessels, have broad, ribbon-like hyphae with few or no septa that branch at wide angles, often near 90 degrees, and are linked to diabetic ketoacidosis. In people with normal immunity, Aspergillus can instead colonize an old tuberculous cavity as a fungus ball or, in asthma and cystic fibrosis, provoke an IgE-mediated and immune complex reaction (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis).
Pneumocystis

Pneumocystis jirovecii, formerly called P. carinii (a name now kept for the rat species), is a fungus by ribosomal RNA and genome analysis, although its membrane contains cholesterol rather than ergosterol. CD4 T cells normally recruit and activate the macrophages that clear it. When the CD4 count falls below about 200 cells/mm3, organisms multiply while attached to type I pneumocytes, and alveoli fill with a foamy exudate of organisms, surfactant, and protein. This thickens the gas exchange barrier and fills alveoli, causing dry cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia with a widened alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient that worsens with exertion. Imaging shows bilateral interstitial or ground-glass infiltrates, and serum lactate dehydrogenase rises with lung cell injury. Silver stain of induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid reveals the cysts.

blocks.predict: Two patients have fungal pneumonia: one is receiving chemotherapy with an absolute neutrophil count near zero, the other has untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 60 cells/mm3. Which organism fits each, and what would a biopsy or lavage show?
blocks.explain: Neutropenia removes the hyphae-killing cell, so Aspergillus with septate, acute-angle hyphae invading vessels fits the first. Loss of CD4 T cells fits Pneumocystis, with silver-stained cysts in foamy alveolar exudate.
blocks.check: Compare with the comparison table and the Aspergillus and Pneumocystis paragraphs.

integration.text: Every pathogen in this chapter defeats a particular layer of lung defense, and the host who gets it is the host missing that layer. Capsules defeat complement and phagocytosis, so asplenia and antibody or complement defects favor S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae type b. Loss of mucociliary clearance from influenza, smoking, cystic fibrosis, or an endotracheal tube opens the lower airway to S. aureus, Pseudomonas, and other bacteria. Intracellular survivors (M. tuberculosis, Legionella, Histoplasma) require Th1 cells, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha, so they emerge with HIV, glucocorticoids, or TNF blockade, while neutropenia favors Aspergillus and CD4 depletion favors Pneumocystis. Biochemistry explains toxins (ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 or Gi) and culture needs (heme, NAD+, iron, cysteine), and pathology shows the host response as consolidation, granulomas, syncytia, or infarction.

These associations are probabilities, not rules. A patient with HIV can still get pneumococcal pneumonia, and a healthy traveler can develop histoplasmosis after a heavy exposure. Stains and colony traits support identification, but molecular tests and antigen assays now often confirm it, and some classic tests (such as the Legionella urine antigen) detect only part of a species. Board questions reward linking organism biology to host defect; real diagnosis integrates exposure, host, imaging, and laboratory evidence.

summary: S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus, alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, and bile soluble; its capsule resists complement and phagocytosis, so asplenia predisposes to sepsis.
Lobar pneumonia progresses through congestion, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution, which explain rusty sputum, consolidation signs, and shunt hypoxemia.

H. influenzae needs factors X (hemin) and V (NAD+); Klebsiella has a thick capsule and follows aspiration in alcohol use; Pseudomonas is oxidase positive and colonizes cystic fibrosis airways and ventilator tubing; Legionella grows on charcoal yeast extract with iron and cysteine and comes from contaminated water.
Diphtheria toxin is phage-encoded and ADP-ribosylates EF-2, stopping protein synthesis, producing a pseudomembrane, myocarditis, and neuropathy.
Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi so it cannot inhibit adenylyl cyclase; cAMP rises, causing lymphocytosis and phagocyte dysfunction, while ciliary damage drives the paroxysmal cough.

M. tuberculosis is acid-fast because of mycolic acids, spreads by droplet nuclei, survives in macrophages by blocking phagolysosome fusion, and is controlled by Th1 cells, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha within granulomas.
Influenza hemagglutinin binds sialic acid and neuraminidase releases virions; drift is point mutation, shift is segment reassortment in influenza A only.
RSV F protein forms syncytia and causes infant bronchiolitis; SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped positive-sense RNA virus whose spike binds ACE2.
Histoplasma (small yeasts in macrophages), Blastomyces (broad-based budding yeast), and Coccidioides (spherules with endospores) are identified by geography and tissue form.
Aspergillus (septate acute-angle hyphae) invades vessels when neutrophils fail; Pneumocystis (silver-stained cysts) fills alveoli when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/mm3.

verify: Timing of the stages of lobar pneumonia varies slightly between editions of Robbins and review texts; values here are stated as approximate.
The number of pneumococcal capsular serotypes is given as more than 90 or about 100 in different sources.
The mechanism of hyponatremia in Legionnaires disease is not settled (inappropriate ADH secretion is commonly cited); confirm how NABNE frames it.
Durations of the pertussis stages vary between sources (paroxysmal stage given as 2 to 6 weeks or up to 10 weeks).

M. tuberculosis generation time (about 15 to 20 hours) and the roles assigned to individual wall lipids (cord factor, sulfatides, lipoarabinomannan) differ in emphasis between microbiology and immunology texts.
RSV taxonomy changed in 2016 (family Pneumoviridae, genus Orthopneumovirus); confirm whether NABNE items still classify it as a paramyxovirus.
Fungal sizes (Histoplasma about 2 to 4 um, Blastomyces about 8 to 15 um, Coccidioides spherules about 20 to 60 um or larger) are approximate and vary by source.
The neutrophil count that defines high risk for invasive aspergillosis (commonly below about 500 cells/uL, especially when prolonged beyond about 10 days) should be confirmed if tested.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms and test names quellung, Elek test, Ghon complex, Bordet-Gengou, and Regan-Lowe.
